query: What psychometric specifications (item counts, reliability targets, construct validity checks), sample sizes, and mediation models will link training uptake to compliance outcomes and detect knowledge-retention differences?

response.query: What psychometric specifications (item counts, reliability targets, construct validity checks), sample sizes, and mediation models will link training uptake to compliance outcomes and detect knowledge-retention differences?
response.answer: For linking training uptake to compliance outcomes, use a minimum of 300 participants, reliability targets of Cronbach’s alpha > 0.7, and mediation models like Baron-Kenny or bootstrapping for analysis. Construct validity checks are essential to ensure measurement accuracy.

results.title: Reliability and Validity | Test Partnership
results.content: # Reliability and Validity. **Reliability and validity are critical in ensuring results are dependable and measure what they are supposed to. Whereas validity refers to whether a tool measures what it is intended to measure and whether the results are meaningful and applicable to the concept being studied.**. Put simply, reliability relates to the precision, accuracy, and replicability of psychometric test scores. For example, if a student completes a psychometric assessment 10 times, and gets the exact same score each time, the assessment can be said to show “reliability”. However, more investigation is required to determine if the scores themselves are meaningful, and measure the psychological construct it purports to measure. **To show that a test is “valid”, multiple forms of validation are required, especially for newer assessments and less established psychological constructs.** As part of the R&D process for psychometric assessments, psychometricians conduct many studies investigating the reliability and validity of the assessment, presenting the findings in a technical manual or academic journal article.

results.title: Psychometric characteristics of the n-back task: Construct validity across age and stimulus type, internal consistency, test-retest and alternate forms reliability | Current Psychology | Springer Nature Link
results.content:
Title: Psychometric characteristics of the n-back task: Construct validity across age and stimulus type, internal consistency, test-retest and alternate forms reliability | Current Psychology | Springer Nature Link
# Psychometric characteristics of the *n*-back task: Construct validity across age and stimulus type, internal consistency, test-retest and alternate forms reliability. Psychometric characteristics of the *n*-back task: Construct validity across age and stimulus type, internal consistency, test-retest and alternate forms reliability. In this study, we comprehensively examined the psychometric properties of the *n*-back task by evaluating its construct validity across different age groups (younger and older adults) and stimulus types (verbal and non-verbal) and by assessing reliability through three methods: test-retest, split-half, and alternate forms. Studies employing the *n*-back task show that older adults exhibit increased response times and errors under higher WM loads, highlighting age-related cognitive impairments (Vaughan et al., 2008. Building on this, Study 1 of the current research investigates the construct validity of the *n*-back task by examining its ability to detect group differences using the known-groups method, comparing younger and older adults with verbal (letters) and non-verbal (shapes) stimuli. Evidence for construct validity would be provided if *n*-back performance differs by age but remains similar between verbal and non-verbal stimuli, with no expected age-related differences in discrimination ability and RT between stimulus types. Evidence for the *n*-back task’s construct validity was expected to be found in the similarity of performance across age groups in the discrimination of targets from non-targets for verbal and non-verbal stimuli in all *n*-back conditions. To provide evidence for the construct validity of the *n*-back task, we expected similar verbal and non-verbal *n*-back task performance for both younger and older adults but differentiated performance favouring the younger age group. It is important to note that instead of assessing the *n*-back task’s consistency solely based on individual working memory (WM) loads, we analyzed its reliability across time, task halves, and forms using four parameters: mean accuracy and reaction time for both target and non-target measures. Our study provides evidence that the *n*-back is a highly reliable task and demonstrates construct validity, supporting its use with both verbal and non-verbal stimuli across younger and older adults for assessing WM performance. Psychometric characteristics of the *n*-back task: Construct validity across age and stimulus type, internal consistency, test-retest and alternate forms reliability.

results.title: Evaluating the reliability and validity of SF-8 with a large representative sample of urban Chinese | Health and Quality of Life Outcomes | Springer Nature Link
results.content:
Title: Evaluating the reliability and validity of SF-8 with a large representative sample of urban Chinese | Health and Quality of Life Outcomes | Springer Nature Link
# Evaluating the reliability and validity of SF-8 with a large representative sample of urban Chinese. The Short Form-8 (SF-8) is a widely used instrument for measuring health-related quality of life (HRQOL). The purpose of the current study is to evaluate the reliability and validity of the Chinese version SF-8 using a large, representative sample of city residents in mainland China. Internal consistency reliability of the SF-8 was evaluated with item-total correlations and Cronbach’s alphas. Construct validity was assessed with factor analysis. Known-groups validity was examined based on known HRQOL differences in age, gender, income, and overall quality of life. We showed that SF-8 has very good internal consistency reliability and known-groups validity. Our results also confirmed that the traditional 2-factor structure of SF-8 (physical and mental health) is reasonable among Chinese city residents. Further, we showed that a 3-factor model (physical, mental, and overall health) fit the data better than the traditional 2-factor model. This study is the first to confirm the traditional 2-factor structure of SF-8 using a large, representative sample from China. Future studies may further explore the possibility of a 3-factor structure for the SF-8 among the Chinese population. ### Confirmatory and bi-factor analysis of the Short Form Health Survey 8 (SF-8) scale structure in a German general population sample. ### Psychometric properties of the Chinese version of the SF-36v2 in patients with severe mental illnesses in China: factor structure, reliability, and validity. With 36 questions, it takes on average 17 min to complete the SF-36 survey when administered via telephone by experienced interviewers [5 and short form 12-item (SF-12) health surveys, Nottingham health profile (NHP), sickness impact profile (SIP), medical outcomes study short form 6D (SF-6D), health utilities index mark 3 (HUI3), quality of well-being scale (QWB), and assessment of quality of life (AQoL). Using a random sample of 1517 participants, the authors showed that the SF-8 Chinese version has good internal consistency reliability (overall Cronbach’s alpha = 0.749) and criterion validity (correlation between the SF-8 and SF-36 was 0.559) [12]. Thus, in the current study, we extend the psychometric testing of the Chinese version SF-8 by assessing its internal consistency reliability, construct validity, and known-groups validity using a larger, more representative sample of Chinese city residents.
